title: The Next Compact
author: How to Teach With AI
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), August 10, 2026
summary: This piece from How to Teach With AI is an unusual hybrid: the author asked Claude to write, without constraints, a full essay answering 'What should the next compact for colleges look like?' as part of a four-day experiment ahead of the Chronicle of Higher Education's fall festival, then wrapped it in his own critical framing. Claude's essay argues that America renegotiates its social compact with higher education roughly once a generation — citing the 1862 land-grant act, the 1944 GI Bill, the 1947-1972 mass-access era, and Pell Grants — and that the current 1972-era compact (access to credentials financed by debt, on the assumption a degree reliably converts to a better life) has quietly expired, evidenced by collapsing public confidence, rising graduate underemployment, and AI-driven entry-level job losses concentrated among 22-to-25-year-olds. It rejects three 'bad compacts' currently on offer (a government loyalty compact, a nostalgic restoration of the old deal, and a fully unbundled 'vending machine' credential market) in favor of eight proposed articles: colleges would certify competency rather than seat-time, share financial risk with students, serve lifelong learners, teach AI fluency alongside deliberately AI-free assessment, and choose institutional neutrality — while society, in turn, would fund research as insulated public good, treat academic autonomy as an operating condition rather than a reward, and end employer free-riding on training costs. The author's own framing is skeptical but genuinely unsettled: he flags the essay's flattering rhetoric and unverifiable statistics as real weaknesses, but says no human-authored strategic document he's encountered has been this coherent about what higher education owes the public.
points: The historical framework — that the U.S. has renegotiated its higher-ed compact roughly once a generation (1862 land-grant, 1944 GI Bill, 1947-1972 mass access, Pell Grants) — reframes the current crisis as an overdue renegotiation rather than a permanent decline, since the prior compact is now over fifty years old.

The AI-specific data point is the sharpest evidence for urgency: Stanford's Digital Economy Lab found employment for 22-to-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations dropped 13-16% since late 2022 while older workers in the same jobs held steady — meaning AI is hollowing out exactly the entry-level rung the bachelor's degree was built to reach.

Article 1's proposed fix — replacing credit-hour seat-time with competency certification via oral defense and portfolios — is framed as reviving medieval and pre-modern assessment methods (the viva) precisely because they are the hardest to fake with AI.

The essay's own author flags its central weakness in real time: the skills-based hiring revolution its 'vending-machine compact' critique leans on 'changed fewer than 1 in 700 actual hires' according to Harvard/Burning Glass research — meaning employers who claim to have moved past degrees mostly haven't changed their actual hiring practice.
quotes: America rewrites its deal with college roughly once a generation. The last rewrite was fifty years ago. Everyone is now fighting over the corpse of the old one — and nobody is drafting the new one.
a diploma should stop being a receipt and become a warrant. We watched her do it. We challenged her on it. We are staking our name on her.

Fifty-two percent of four-year graduates are underemployed a year after graduation. For the first time in the modern record, recent college graduates have a higher unemployment rate than the workforce as a whole.

Stanford's Digital Economy Lab found that employment for 22-to-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations has dropped roughly 13-16% since late 2022, while older workers in the same jobs held steady.

What's scarce is proof. Proof that a human being can actually do what their credential claims. Proof that an institution's promises mean something. The old compact traded access for money. The next compact must trade proof for trust.
Registered apprenticeships have doubled in a decade to 680,000 — a start, and still a rounding error against 15 million undergraduates.
Incumbents have never written the next compact. A shopkeeper's son wrote the land-grant deal. The American Legion drafted the GI Bill. Governors invented WGU.
